items.title: Around 700,000 displaced amid volatile conflict in southern Ethiopia, Islamic Relief says
items.author: Islamic Relief
items.content:
Countries: Ethiopia, Kenya
Source: Islamic Relief

Almost 700,000 people have been displaced amid an escalation of conflict in southern Ethiopia along the Kenya, Somalia, Ethiopia border as aid agencies prepare to respond, Islamic Relief says.

The fighting began on 22 October between Somali and Oromo communities, two ethnic groups living in Ethiopia. The epicentre of the conflict is Moyale a border town projected to be increasingly wealthy as trade grows between Kenya and Ethiopia with the two groups fighting for land.

The conflict has spread up to 300km from the town with fighting breaking out in areas across the ethnic group settlements. Approximately 329,000 people have been displaced from the Somali Region Dawa Zone and 359,798 people were displaced across Southern Oromia. Access to the locations has been challenging but aid agencies have had reports that a humanitarian response is necessary.

Hundreds of thousands of displaced people will need support before they can return to their homes. The conflict has caused the destruction and burning of homes, businesses and fuel stations, significant disruption of health, nutrition, water and sanitation services; and civilians are vulnerable to attack.

Approximately 50,000 people have crossed the Ethiopian border into Kenya seeking safety and humanitarian assistance placing additional pressure on local services and host communities.

Islamic Relief Ethiopia head of programmes, Kedir Musema Hameza said:

“This is a volatile conflict driven by two ethnic groups competing for land and wealth in the borders of Ethiopia. Unfortunately when conflict like this arises it is vulnerable civilians that end up paying a high price. We are seeing that now with this mass displacement of nearly 700,000 people fleeing the violence. This is a serious humanitarian incident which we are working to respond to.”

“Homes have been burnt and peoples lives have been hit. We need funding to respond and help these suffering communities. We have reports from local sources that fighting has stopped and UN teams are travelling to assess the condition of the displaced population and the damage.”

Islamic Relief is working to respond including with cash assistance for affected and displaced people, hygiene kits, community and psychosocial support to communities in conflict hit locations of Ethiopia.

items.title: Haiti: Kenscoff violence highlights continued risk of killing, abduction and other abuses against children by gangs – new research
items.author: Amnesty International
items.content:
Country: Haiti
Source: Amnesty International

Children in Haiti remain at risk of killings, abductions, sexual violence and other abuses by armed gangs, Amnesty International said in new research ahead of World Children’s Day.

Amnesty International interviewed witnesses to the Kenscoff gang raid on 23 August 2026, in which 55 people were killed and 15 more were injured, according to a municipal official. The UN said at least three boys and two girls were among those killed. A further 67 people, including 13 children, were abducted, according to municipal data.

Witnesses told Amnesty International that the attack began when dozens of gang members raided various parts of the commune of Kenscoff, south of Port-au-Prince. They attacked people in their homes, shooting them and setting houses on fire. They looted belongings and shot residents as they tried to escape. They also attacked displaced people who were taking shelter in the Ark of the New Covenant Church and shot many of them.

Children’s lives have been devastated by these horrors

Scott Edwards, Director of Amnesty International’s Crisis Response Programme

“Survivors of the Kenscoff August attack, which came just weeks after another massacre in the same commune, described how they watched as gang members killed their relatives and friends, and how they were raped, beaten and abducted,” said Scott Edwards, Director of Amnesty International’s Crisis Response Programme.

“Children’s lives have been devastated by these horrors. Survivors must have access to mental health support and necessary protection services.

“On World Children’s Day, we are again calling for the Haitian authorities and the international community to urgently increase efforts to protect Haiti’s children as escalating gang violence continues to threaten their lives. Additionally, intensified security operations must not expose children to further harm.”

World Children’s Day, celebrated annually on 20 November, marks the anniversary of the adoption of the Convention on the Rights of the Child (CRC), which outlines the rights of every child and what governments must do to protect them. Haiti is a state party to the CRC.

Kenscoff attacks

Organized gangs – namely Grand Ravine, Ti Bwa, 5 Segon and 400 Mawozo – started attacking the mountainous commune of Kenscoff in January 2025. All four gangs are part of the Viv Ansanm coalition.

Kenscoff borders Pétion-Ville, where many government offices, embassies and key commercial interests are situated. The 23 August attack on the population, which began around 9pm and was primarily led by a group from the 5 Segon gang, further appeared to be a retaliation for intensified security operations against the gangs.

One teenage girl told Amnesty International that she hid under her bed as gunshots rang out: “When they came inside the house, they said everybody should get out [or else] they would kill us.”

The girl was abducted and held for a little over one month alongside other abductees: “They [gang members] threatened us a lot… They came in and told us that they didn’t come all this way, risking death, for us to think that nothing would happen to us. They threatened that they would kill us.”

According to the UN, 15 women and four girls were raped. One teenage girl, who was abducted and raped, told Amnesty International: “We heard gunshots, but we didn’t have anywhere to go. We didn’t know where to go… They came in [to our house] and took everybody.”

The girl was tied up with an extension cord and beaten. She was separated from her family, and raped by two gang members on a street: “I tried to fight, but they hit me with a hammer and ripped my underwear… They tied me to a pole and told me they were going to fight with the police… The way they tied me was kind of loose. I freed myself and fled.”

One man who was among the displaced people sheltering in the church said gang members shot and killed one of his family members, a mother of two, as she tried to flee. He managed to hide alongside the two children, but one, a teenage boy, ran to a nearby burial site and was shot. The next morning, the man emerged from hiding and saw that the boy had been shot four times. The boy spent more than two weeks in hospital recovering. The man said of the boy’s condition after the attack: “He has some difficulty adapting at school… he forgets everything.”

Abduction by gangs

Amnesty International documented the abduction of at least 11 children, including three toddlers. Abductees said they were tied up and forced to walk in the dark for hours to houses that gang members had occupied.

Abductees were made to sleep on the floor. One girl said the room where she was initially held was overcrowded, so abductees had to take turns to lie down. They were given very little to eat – mostly crackers, and rice and beans – and untreated water to drink.

Abductees who escaped after security operations faced further hardship and danger as they were caught in resulting aerial attacks, including drone strikes. One girl said she ran barefoot for two days to escape, using her t-shirt to bandage her wounded feet.

The girl said she witnessed at least two boys abducted alongside her die after being injured by the drone strikes. These testimonies are a reminder to Haitian security authorities and their partners – including mercenaries, Salvadoran troops and the UN-backed Gang Suppression Force – of the importance of ensuring that members of the population are spared during security operations.

Witnesses said gang members requested money in exchange for the release of some abductees. Some family members said they simply could not afford to make the ransom payments. At least one family paid close to USD 700 to ensure the release of an adolescent girl, but the gang members didn’t let her go.

On 28 August, UNICEF reported that six children and seven women who were abducted had been released. Others remained in captivity for varying periods, with the whereabouts of some still unknown.

The repeated attacks on Kenscoff have caused multiple waves of displacement. The August attack displaced more than 4,200 people. Interviewees described difficult living conditions in displacement and said many displaced children were struggling to return to school. Insecurity has also disrupted agricultural production in the farming commune.

Community members and Haitian and international human rights monitors criticized the apparent inadequate response of security forces to the attacks.

Need for accountability

Authorities are investigating the Kenscoff violence. They must be transparent about these investigations, and make clear the fate of residents who were caught up in the subsequent security operations.

Previous investigations into various massacres by gangs in recent years have not yet amounted to credible trials. Authorities must ensure that impunity is tackled through independent and impartial investigations that hold to account those suspected of criminal responsibility, including politicians supporting gangs.

“Amnesty International continues to call on the Haitian government and international partners to develop and implement a comprehensive child protection plan, ensuring access to education, healthcare and justice for survivors. Protecting children must be an essential part of any response to Haiti’s security crisis,” said Ana Piquer, Americas Director at Amnesty International.

In the months ahead, Amnesty International will release more outputs based on research conducted between September and November 2026, which included a visit to Haiti and more than 60 interviews. The research is part of the organization’s work on the impact of the crisis on children. Since the assassination of President Jovenel Moïse in July 2021, violence by armed gangs has escalated significantly in Haiti and has amounted to an assault on childhood.

items.title: Afghanistan: Afghan women call for greater opportunities at Global Open Day with SRSG Fatima | United Nations Peace Operations
items.author: UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan
items.content:
Country: Afghanistan
Source: UN Assistance Mission in Afghanistan

KABUL- Afghan women leaders, journalists, entrepreneurs and civil society representatives met with the Special Representative of the Secretary-General and Head of UNAMA, Rabab Fatima, during a United Nations-supported Global Open Day event in Kabul, calling for greater opportunities and meaningful participation for women in Afghan society.

The event brought together around 50 women's rights advocates, media representatives, business leaders, and community members to discuss the challenges facing Afghan women and girls and exchange ideas on how to address them.

In her remarks, Fatima commended the contributions of Afghan women. "Across the country, I have seen the determination, contribution and leadership of women," she said, emphasising that women do not want to be passive recipients of support but active participants in shaping the decisions and policies that affect their lives.

Participants stressed the importance of ensuring women's meaningful participation in public life, including access to education, employment and other fundamental rights. Their calls come amid continued restrictions on women and girls. As of 2026, an estimated 2.4 million girls remain excluded from secondary education, reversing two decades of progress in expanding access to learning opportunities.

"What will happen to Afghanistan in 20 years without educated women?" asked one participant.

Launched by the United Nations Security Council in 2010, Global Open Day events are held worldwide to promote dialogue between United Nations representatives and women's organizations, raise awareness of women's contributions to peace and security, and support their participation in conflict prevention and resolution.

items.title: Nepal: Au milieu des souffrances causées par les inondations, une clinique d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge contribue à faire naître de nouvelles vies au Népal. | IFRC
items.author: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies
items.content:
Country: Nepal
Source: International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies

Par Fleur Verwer, IFRC coordinator à l'IFRC pour l’opération d’urgence liée aux inondations au Népal.

---

La clinique d’urgence de la Société de la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) venait tout juste d’ouvrir ses portes pour la journée lorsqu’une jeune femme enceinte et son compagnon s’y sont présentés. Ses vêtements étaient trempés, elle souffrait énormément et ne savait pas quoi faire.

Se rendre à l’hôpital était impossible : les eaux de crue avaient emporté le pont qui y menait, et elle ne pouvait pas traverser la rivière.

Ayant entendu parler de la clinique d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge, elle avait décidé de s’y rendre pour chercher de l’aide.

Le Dr Gyanendra Jora était de garde lorsque la jeune femme est arrivée.

« Elle n’avait que 18 ans et ne savait manifestement pas quoi faire. Elle nous a expliqué que sa poche des eaux s’était rompue brusquement la veille », se souvient-il.

Pour le Dr Jora, il était immédiatement évident qu’il fallait agir sans perdre de temps. Après un examen rapide de la mère et du bébé, il a organisé son transfert en urgence vers un centre d’accouchement, où elle pourrait bénéficier d'un suivi médical et accoucher en toute sécurité.

Le Dr Gyanendra Jora devant la clinique médicale d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge népalaise à Bidur, où il a travaillé pendant plusieurs semaines après les inondations.

Photo: IFRC

Moins d’une demi-heure après son arrivée, la jeune femme était déjà en route. Le Dr Jora, accompagné d’une infirmière de la Société de la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) et d’un volontaire, l’a escortée à bord d’une ambulance de la CRN jusqu’à un centre de santé urbain situé à environ 25 kilomètres. Son travail était déjà bien avancé et chaque minute comptait. Une trentaine de minutes plus tard, l’équipe l’a confiée au personnel du centre d’accouchement, s’est assurée qu’elle était entre de bonnes mains, puis est retournée à la clinique.

Trois heures et demie plus tard, une petite fille en bonne santé venait au monde.

Lorsque la nouvelle de la naissance est parvenue à la clinique, un immense soulagement a envahi l’équipe qui avait pris cette première décision déterminante.

Plus tard, une équipe de l'IFRC et de la CRN, comprenant Sachiko Kawase, déléguée Santé de l’IFRC, s’est rendue auprès de la mère et de son nouveau-né pour prendre de leurs nouvelles. Elle a constaté que le bébé était en bonne santé et se portait bien.

Pour accompagner la famille dans les jours à venir, l’équipe a remis à la mère un kit de dignité, comprenant notamment un foulard pour le bébé, ainsi qu’un kit d’hygiène. Cette visite constituait la dernière étape d’une chaîne de soins : du premier examen médical au transport en ambulance, jusqu’à cette visite de suivi, la Croix-Rouge avait accompagné la famille à chaque étape.

Au milieu du deuil, de la douleur et des pertes causés par les inondations, cette nouvelle vie a fait naître une lueur d’espoir.

Un membre de la Croix-Rouge népalaise examine une femme à la clinique, qui a pris en charge plus de 1 500 personnes en 24 jours.

Photo: IFRC

Un soutien vital après les inondations

L’histoire de cette jeune mère n’est qu’une parmi tant d’autres qui se sont déroulées à la clinique d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge à Bidur.

Après les inondations dévastatrices du 26 août, la ville s’est retrouvée largement coupée des services de santé. Le pont qui reliait l’hôpital public à l’autre partie de la ville a été emporté par la violence des eaux. Les personnes qui dépendaient de cet hôpital pour obtenir des médicaments, bénéficier de soins gratuits ou recevoir une assistance médicale d’urgence se sont soudainement retrouvées sans solution.

Pour maintenir l’accès aux soins de santé essentiels, la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) a mis en place cette clinique d’urgence, devenue indispensable.

La clinique n’était pas nouvelle, mais son rôle était plus crucial que jamais. Elle avait été déployée pour la première fois après le séisme de 2015 au Népal. Une fois encore, elle a constitué un maillon essentiel de la réponse, faisant toute la différence entre avoir accès aux soins de santé de base et en être totalement privé.

Au cours des 24 jours de fonctionnement de la clinique, les médecins ont pris en charge plus de 1 500 personnes présentant des problèmes de santé très variés : des affections bénignes aux maladies chroniques, comme l’hypertension artérielle et la bronchopneumopathie chronique obstructive, en passant par des cas nécessitant une orientation urgente vers un hôpital.

Des membres de la Croix-Rouge népalaise apportent leur aide à deux personnes touchées par les inondations au niveau de la pharmacie de la clinique.

Photo: IFRC

Soutenir la communauté

Âgée de 17 ans, Isha, volontaire de la Croix-Rouge, était présente dès le premier jour d’ouverture de la clinique après les inondations.

« J’habite juste derrière la clinique. Heureusement, ma maison n’a pas été touchée par les inondations et ma famille est en sécurité. Lorsque j’ai appris que la clinique d’urgence était en cours d’installation, j’ai immédiatement voulu apporter mon aide. J’ai assisté le pharmacien et contribué à alléger sa charge de travail », raconte Isha.

Les volontaires comme Isha n’étaient pas les seuls à se dévouer pleinement. Le Dr Jora, qui a travaillé à la clinique pendant plusieurs semaines, ne s’est pas contenté de soigner les patients : il leur a également prêté une oreille attentive et a été profondément touché par les témoignages qu’ils lui ont confiés.

« Je savais que j’étais là pour fournir des soins médicaux, mais les histoires que les gens me racontaient m’ont profondément marqué. Tant de personnes portaient en elles une immense souffrance. Pas seulement physique, mais aussi émotionnelle », confie le Dr Jora.

Il se souvient notamment d’un homme qui avait subi trois crises convulsives successives, chacune durant plusieurs minutes.

Le chemin vers le rétablissement

La CRN a également rétabli l’accès à l’eau potable pour plus de 13 900 personnes et fourni des premiers secours psychologiques ainsi qu’un soutien psychosocial à plus de 1 700 autres personnes. À Bidur, elle a été la première organisation à commencer à fournir une assistance financière aux familles dans le besoin.

La clinique d’urgence de la Société de la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) venait tout juste d’ouvrir ses portes pour la journée lorsqu’une jeune femme enceinte et son compagnon s’y sont présentés. Ses vêtements étaient trempés, elle souffrait énormément et ne savait pas quoi faire.
Se rendre à l’hôpital était impossible : les eaux de crue avaient emporté le pont qui y menait, et elle ne pouvait pas traverser la rivière.
Ayant entendu parler de la clinique d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge, elle avait décidé de s’y rendre pour chercher de l’aide.
Le Dr Gyanendra Jora était de garde lorsque la jeune femme est arrivée.
« Elle n’avait que 18 ans et ne savait manifestement pas quoi faire. Elle nous a expliqué que sa poche des eaux s’était rompue brusquement la veille », se souvient-il.
Pour le Dr Jora, il était immédiatement évident qu’il fallait agir sans perdre de temps. Après un examen rapide de la mère et du bébé, il a organisé son transfert en urgence vers un centre d’accouchement, où elle pourrait bénéficier d'un suivi médical et accoucher en toute sécurité.
Le Dr Gyanendra Jora devant la clinique médicale d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge népalaise à Bidur, où il a travaillé pendant plusieurs semaines après les inondations.

Moins d’une demi-heure après son arrivée, la jeune femme était déjà en route. Le Dr Jora, accompagné d’une infirmière de la Société de la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) et d’un volontaire, l’a escortée à bord d’une ambulance de la CRN jusqu’à un centre de santé urbain situé à environ 25 kilomètres. Son travail était déjà bien avancé et chaque minute comptait. Une trentaine de minutes plus tard, l’équipe l’a confiée au personnel du centre d’accouchement, s’est assurée qu’elle était entre de bonnes mains, puis est retournée à la clinique.
Trois heures et demie plus tard, une petite fille en bonne santé venait au monde.
Lorsque la nouvelle de la naissance est parvenue à la clinique, un immense soulagement a envahi l’équipe qui avait pris cette première décision déterminante.
Plus tard, une équipe de l'IFRC et de la CRN, comprenant Sachiko Kawase, déléguée Santé de l’IFRC, s’est rendue auprès de la mère et de son nouveau-né pour prendre de leurs nouvelles. Elle a constaté que le bébé était en bonne santé et se portait bien.
Pour accompagner la famille dans les jours à venir, l’équipe a remis à la mère un kit de dignité, comprenant notamment un foulard pour le bébé, ainsi qu’un kit d’hygiène. Cette visite constituait la dernière étape d’une chaîne de soins : du premier examen médical au transport en ambulance, jusqu’à cette visite de suivi, la Croix-Rouge avait accompagné la famille à chaque étape.
Au milieu du deuil, de la douleur et des pertes causés par les inondations, cette nouvelle vie a fait naître une lueur d’espoir.
Un membre de la Croix-Rouge népalaise examine une femme à la clinique, qui a pris en charge plus de 1 500 personnes en 24 jours.
Photo: IFRC
Un soutien vital après les inondations
L’histoire de cette jeune mère n’est qu’une parmi tant d’autres qui se sont déroulées à la clinique d’urgence de la Croix-Rouge à Bidur.
Après les inondations dévastatrices du 26 août, la ville s’est retrouvée largement coupée des services de santé. Le pont qui reliait l’hôpital public à l’autre partie de la ville a été emporté par la violence des eaux. Les personnes qui dépendaient de cet hôpital pour obtenir des médicaments, bénéficier de soins gratuits ou recevoir une assistance médicale d’urgence se sont soudainement retrouvées sans solution.
Pour maintenir l’accès aux soins de santé essentiels, la Croix-Rouge népalaise (CRN) a mis en place cette clinique d’urgence, devenue indispensable.
La clinique n’était pas nouvelle, mais son rôle était plus crucial que jamais. Elle avait été déployée pour la première fois après le séisme de 2015 au Népal. items.title: World: ICRC: Landmines, booby-traps and other devices continue to inflict grave suffering on civilians
items.author: International Committee of the Red Cross
items.content:
Country: World
Source: International Committee of the Red Cross

Statement on the Occasion of the 28th Annual Conference of the High Contracting Parties to Amended Protocol II on Prohibitions or Restrictions on the Use of Mines, Booby-Traps and Other Devices, 13 November 2026

In far too many places around the world, everyday activities like driving to the market, walking to school, playing outdoors, cultivating land or herding animals, and even handling ordinary devices entail deadly risks.

Landmines, booby-traps and other devices continue to inflict grave suffering on civilians. They impede access to health-care facilities and other essential services, and hamper humanitarian operations. Even once the fighting has ended, these weapons leave behind long-term explosive hazards that impede the safe return of displaced populations and hinder reconstruction and development.

Year after year, mines, booby-traps and other explosive devices claim thousands of lives. According to the Landmine Monitor 2025, the overwhelming majority of victims are civilians, many of them children – the very people who must never be attacked and must be protected from the dangers of military operations. Last year alone, ICRC teams in 28 countries provided physical rehabilitation services for more than 25,000 people suffering with often life-altering injuries because of mines, cluster munitions and other explosive remnants of war. Many of those we treat are grappling with debilitating physical injuries that also have psychological and financial impacts.

The ICRC is particularly concerned about the dramatic increase in the use of anti-personnel landmines – both manufactured and improvised – including on the territories of High Contracting Parties.

Anti-personnel mines have indiscriminate effects. The ICRC and the wider International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement, along with states party to the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention, condemn the use of anti-personnel mines by any actor, and the ICRC urges all those who continue to use anti-personnel mines to cease such use immediately. We recall in this connection that High Contracting Parties bound by both the Protocol and the Anti-Personnel Mine Ban Convention are prohibited from using anti-personnel mines in all circumstances. We urge High Contracting Parties to give effect to relevant prohibitions and restrictions in their domestic legislation and military instructions, and to reflect these measures in their National Annual Reports submitted under the Protocol.

In addition, we call on all those who use anti-vehicle mines to step up their efforts significantly to protect civilians against their indiscriminate effects. The ICRC has long called for the rules of international law applicable to such mines to be strengthened to enhance the protection of civilians. An anti-vehicle mine (AV mine) does not distinguish between a military, civilian or humanitarian vehicle. Consequently, AV mines can considerably hinder the delivery of humanitarian assistance to vulnerable populations. They can also hamper the return of displaced civilians, the cultivation of valuable farmland and reconstruction efforts at the end of active hostilities. Further steps are needed to effectively address the harm caused to civilians by anti-vehicle mines.

Such steps could include, for example, the High Contracting Parties that endorsed the 2006 Declaration on Anti-vehicle Mines using the opportunity of this Review Conference and subsequent meetings of High Contracting Parties to report on their implementation of the Declaration’s commitments. This could also include confirmation that these commitments are now part of military doctrine and policy.

High Contracting Parties must strictly comply with the requirements of Amended Protocol II and its Annex. Recording, retaining and sharing information concerning minefields, mined areas, mines, booby-traps and other devices, as required by Article 9, is key to the implementation of life-saving measures. Another notable obligation is the removal of mines without delay after the cessation of active hostilities, in line with Article 10. States party to both Protocols II and V can develop a joint system to implement the two Protocols and make the process less resource intensive. Helpful guidance is available in the Technical Annex to Protocol V and in the ICRC’s briefing note on preventing and eradicating the deadly legacy of explosive remnants of war.

Madam President,

Today, the ICRC partners with 20 National Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, with more than 2,100 staff and volunteers, working alongside communities to help reduce their exposure to the risks posed by mines, cluster munitions and other explosive remnants of war. This work includes technical support in clearance operations, raising awareness of and promoting safer behaviour, physical rehabilitation services, and support for the social and economic inclusion of survivors.

For the protection of civilians, it remains critically important that Amended Protocol II is universally adhered to. We encourage all High Contracting Parties to redouble their efforts to promote its universalization and we call on states that have not already joined the Protocol to do so without further delay.

items.title: oPt: West Bank Protection Cluster Snapshot | Protection Monitoring | Reporting Period 1 Aug – 30 Sept 2026
items.author: Protection Cluster
items.content:
Country: occupied Palestinian territory
Sources: Protection Cluster, UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights

Please refer to the attached file.

INTRODUCTION

Findings from August–September 2026 highlight the combined impact of settler violence, movement restrictions, demolitions, and loss of land and property on the safety, livelihoods, and wellbeing of communities across the West Bank. The highest protection risk severity scores were recorded for attacks on civilians and civilian objects, including unlawful killings (58%); theft, extortion, forced eviction or destruction of personal property (58%); and restrictions on freedom of movement, siege and forced displacement (57%). These findings reflect continued threats to civilian safety, housing security, and access to essential services.

Qualitative findings from five Focus Group Discussions across Hebron, Ramallah, Jericho, and Jerusalem governorates highlight settler violence and lack of accountability as central concerns among participating communities. Some groups reported increasing attacks, while others described levels similar to the previous period. Communities reported physical harm, displacement, disrupted education, and persistent psychological distress, with children exposed to unsafe school journeys and young men, including community protection volunteers, facing heightened risks of assault and detention. Women and girls, older persons, and persons with disabilities face additional barriers to safe movement, access to support, and participation in community protection activities. Protection Committees and local networks continue to provide early warning, emergency support, documentation, and legal referrals, although limited resources and threats to responders constrain their efforts.

The Protection Monitoring System (PMS), a joint initiative led by the OPT Protection Cluster, systematically collects, analyzes, and disseminates information on protection risks through Key Informant Interviews (KIIs) and Focus Group Discussions (FGDs), ensuring that community perspectives remain central to the analysis. Building on monitoring undertaken since November 2025, this snapshot presents protection risk severity scores across monitored locations and highlights community-reported concerns, impacts, coping mechanisms, and capacities to inform coordinated protection response and advocacy.

items.title: World: Food Outlook – Biannual report on global food markets, November 2026
items.author: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations
items.content:
Country: World
Source: Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations

Please refer to the attached file.

FAO Food Outlook: Global food commodity supplies remain generally ample, but risks are mounting

New edition examines fertilizer markets, Black Sea export disruptions, and developments in olive oil, whey, and livestock feed costs

Rome – Global agricultural commodity supplies remain generally comfortable, particularly for wheat and coarse grains, although tighter balances are emerging for rice, sugar and vegetable oils. Commodity markets and trade flows nevertheless remain exposed to weather conditions, logistical disruptions and policy uncertainty, according to a new report published today by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO).

The Food Outlook also expects a slowdown in the rate of increase of the global food import bill in 2026, driven largely by lower international prices of coffee and cocoa.

The biannual publication provides updated market assessments and forecasts for the production, utilization, trade, and stocks of major food commodities including cereals, oil crops, sugar, meat, dairy products, fisheries and aquaculture products.

The new edition offers additional insights into fertilizer production, utilization and trade trends, how conflict-driven disruptions in the Black Sea are reshaping trade routes, and special features focusing on whey, olive oil and livestock feed costs.

Key takeaways:

-- Global cereal stocks are forecast to rise by 1.8 percent, by the close of seasons in 2027, largely reflecting an accumulation of wheat inventories in the Russian Federation and Ukraine, where export disruptions are constraining shipments.
--World trade in cereals in 2026/27 is forecast to contract by 3.3 percent, driven almost entirely by a decline in wheat trade, with shipments from all major exporters seen declining. Global trade volumes of rice in 2027 and maize in 2026/27 are expected to expand.
--Global wheat and maize outputs in 2026/27 are anticipated to remain above their respective five-year averages, with global stocks forecast to rise amid constraints on international trade.
--World rice production is forecast to decline for the first time in four seasons, due to falling producer margins and adverse weather conditions associated with El Niño and fall short of utilization; however, large carry-in stocks could keep world rice reserves at their second highest level on record.
--Global production of oilseeds in 2026/27 is expected to expand to record levels, while persistently strong demand for vegetable oils from the biofuel sector will likely lead to a further draw down in global stocks of oils/fats.
--Global meat production is forecast to expand moderately in 2026, led by poultry, while bovine and ovine meat outputs are anticipated to decline amid tight animal availability. Global meat trade is anticipated to grow on firm import demand for poultry meat.
--Global milk production is forecast to expand by 1.8 percent in 2026, while international trade in dairy products is expected to grow by 2.1 percent from the previous year, with stronger shipments of milk powders.
--World sugar production is forecast to decline in 2026/27 and fall below expected global consumption. International sugar prices have risen markedly in recent months, reflecting growing concerns over a tighter global market balance.
--Global fisheries and aquaculture production is set to expand by 0.3 percent in 2026, even as capture production is expected to drop by 3.4 percent, mainly due to El Niño, which is sharply reducing Peruvian anchoveta catches, and higher fuel prices, which are weighing on fleet profitability. Aquaculture production is expected to grow by 3.6 percent, although reduced anchoveta supplies are pushing up feed prices, especially for shrimp and salmon.

Special chapters

The first special feature explores disruptions to fertilizer markets and implications for production and affordability. Global production of nitrogen fertilizers, including ammonia and urea, is expected to decline in 2026, largely reflecting disruptions to energy supplies, production and trade associated with the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. Fertilizer affordability measured relative to crop prices, focusing on maize in Brazil, wheat in the European Union, rice in southeast Asia and soybeans in the United States of America, deteriorated across all four crops and fell below the long-term baseline by mid-2026, reaching its lowest levels between April and June. Elevated fertilizer costs relative to crop prices could weaken farmers' incentives to purchase and apply fertilizers.

Another feature examines how disruptions to Black Sea grain exports are reshaping trade flows. Combined grain shipments from Ukraine's Greater Odesa ports and the Russian Federation's Sea of Azov and Black Sea ports dropped below 0.5 million tonnes in September 2026, from 7.8 million tonnes a year earlier. Accumulating stocks due to export constraints could affect grain quality and marketability issues due to increased pressure on storage capacity. Argentina, Australia and the European Union are increasing their shares of global wheat exports as trade flows adjust to shipping disruptions in the Black Sea region.

A separate feature reviewed recent developments in the global olive oil market. World olive oil production is provisionally forecast to reach a record high of 3.7 million tonnes in 2026/27, with consumption forecast to expand by 6 percent. In Spain, the world’s largest olive oil producer, output is expected to rise by 22.7 percent to 1.6 million tonnes, while wholesale prices of extra virgin olive oil were 18.3 percent lower year on year in September 2026. Meanwhile, prices in Bari, Italy, were more than 50 percent lower year on year.

The report also explores the growing importance of whey. Strong demand for high-protein whey ingredients could increasingly influence the economics of cheese production, as demand for protein for people and livestock adds to the overall value generated from cheese processing. The benefits, however, are likely to be concentrated among processors with access to the necessary whey-processing capacity.

The final feature examines the implications of rising feed costs for livestock producer margins. International prices of key feed ingredients have risen since early 2026, led by oil meals, adding to livestock production costs alongside elevated energy prices. The impact on producer margins varies with output prices, production systems and feed composition. Producers are responding through feed substitution and efficiency gains, although nutritional and economic constraints limit adjustment options.

Food import bill

The new Food Outlook also presents FAO’s estimate for the global food import bill (FIB) in 2026, projected to rise by 1.9 percent to US$ 2.267 trillion, compared with an increase of nearly 8 percent in 2025.

That pace is markedly slower than the previous year, due largely to lower coffee and cocoa prices, even as import bills for cereals and oilseeds are rising again. High-income countries (HICs) are expected to account for 13 percent of the growth, down from 79 percent in 2025, with upper-middle-income countries accounting for about two-thirds, a trend FAO expects to broaden to low- and middle-income economies over the longer term.

The import bill for coffee, tea, cocoa, spices and related products is expected to contract by 11.9 percent in 2026, while the cereal bill is forecast to rise by 3.0 percent, that for oilseeds and oleaginous fruits by 9.9 percent, and the bill for meat products to increase by 6.9 percent.

The overall bill for HICs is expected to edge up by just 0.4 percent in 2026, while that for low- and middle-income economies combined is projected to grow by 4.9 percent, and that for least developed countries to rise by 3.9 percent.

Médecins Sans Frontières' latest report, The burden of occupation, brings together medical data collected between October 2022 and April 2026 in the West Bank, Palestine, alongside patient and staff testimonies from July 2026. The report reveals the profound impact of violence, fear, prolonged adversity, and instability on people’s daily lives and mental health. items.title: Quarter of a Million Landmines Removed from Zimbabwe - The HALO Trust has destroyed four mines per person in north-east Zimbabwe
items.author: HALO Trust
items.content:
Countries: Zimbabwe, Afghanistan, Angola, Colombia, Sri Lanka, Syrian Arab Republic, Ukraine, Yemen
Source: HALO Trust

Harare, Zimbabwe, 19 Nov. The world’s largest landmine clearance charity, the HALO Trust, has reached a significant milestone in Zimbabwe, destroying 250,000 landmines since 2013.

Dense belts of landmines, including the highly sensitive R2M2 models, were laid along Zimbabwe’s borders with Mozambique and Zambia during the Liberation War in the 1970s. They’ve killed or injured more than 1,500 people and 120,000 cattle since independence in 1980.

For 13-years, HALO’s Zimbabwean teams have cleared these minefields in Rushinga and Mount Darwin, saving lives and limbs while restoring farmland, reconnecting communities and laying the foundations for investment and economic growth.

“The destruction of 250,000 landmines is an extraordinary achievement, built on the dedication and courage of Zimbabwean men and women working in some of the country’s most dangerous areas” said Oliver Gerard-Pearse, HALO Trust Zimbabwe Programme Manager.

In Rushinga, where losing a single cow to a landmine can cost a family the equivalent of six months’ school fees, clearance has directly benefited more than 14,000 residents, allowing families to reclaim farmland, graze livestock, grow cash crops and safely access clean water, schools, clinics and markets.

***“We would walk in fear”***saysresidentMunesa Takawira “Now, we are free to walk as we please, and the cows and other domestic animals that used to be hit by landmines can freely move around. We can send children to fetch firewood without fear that they will get injured.”

In Mount Darwin, where HALO became the first operator to hand over an entire district as landmine-free in 2021, deaths and injuries from explosives fell to zero, incomes rose by 90% for nearly a third of local farmers, and land-owning families in six communities increased by more than 80%.

As the largest demining organisation in the country, HALO also provides vital local employment in areas where jobs are scarce. The organisation trains female deminers who are often the main breadwinners for their families and support an average of eight relatives through their clearance work.

Drones, state of the art detectors and mini excavators are helping HALO clear faster and more safely. But technology alone cannot fully counter the impact of sweeping global aid cuts, which threaten Zimbabwe’s aim to achieve mine-free status by 2030.

Just 4% of land remains contaminated says Gerard Pearse who estimates that it would take $6.5 million in donations to free the country from mines by the end of the decade.

“We have seen how safe land can boost investment and development in other countries where HALO works. In neighbouring Mozambique, GDP rose significantly when it was declared mine-free in 2015” he says.

“In Zimbabwe we are now so close to lasting safety for generations to come. We cannot afford to lose momentum at this final stage of a decades-long effort.”

Please find footage of our demining operations here and images here (credit: The HALO Trust)

For more information or to arrange interviews or site visits, please contact media@halotrust.org

Notes to editors

  • Zimbabwe ranked second globally in anti-personnel landmine destruction after Cambodia, according to the Clearing the Mines 2025 report.
  • HALO has trained over 17,000 adults and 73,000 children how to stay safe from explosives since 2015, working closely with Happy Readers, a local charity that provides children with educational books on the risks of mines.
  • HALO also works with Cassim's Prosthetics to support amputees.
  • The HALO Trust is the world's largest humanitarian landmine clearance organisation, working in in 30+ countries including Ukraine, Afghanistan, Yemen, Syria, Colombia, Angola and Sri Lanka.
  • We deploy groundbreaking technology in conflict and post-conflict settings to help people rebuild their homes, restore their livelihoods and keep their children safe.
  • HALO also runs programmes in weapons and ammunition management and safety training. During emergencies, we also provide humanitarian aid and logistical support.
  • HALO was founded in 1988 in Afghanistan.
  • We employ over 8,000 staff worldwide and recruit 95% of them locally.

items.title: Cameroon: North-West and South-West Situation Report No.87, July to September 2026
items.author: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs
items.content:
Country: Cameroon
Source: UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs

Please refer to the attached file.

HIGHLIGHTS

  • More than 1,600 protection incidents recorded in the North-West and South-West regions.
  • Nearly 900 people displaced in the North-West and South-West regions due to violence and insecurity.
  • More than 4,000 people affected by floods and landslides, with about 500 displaced and five deaths reported.
  • Four improvised explosive devices incidents recorded in the North-West region.
  • A total of 736 children with severe acute malnutrition received life-saving treatment in partner-supported treatment centres.

SITUATION OVERVIEW / HUMANITARIAN ACCESS

During the reporting period July-September 2026, the humanitarian situation in Cameroon’s North-West and South-West (NWSW) regions remained fragile and deteriorated further amid continued clashes between State security forces (SSF) and non-State armed groups (NSAGs). Persistent insecurity, including kidnapping for ransom, arbitrary arrests, the proliferation of illegal checkpoints, extortion, and roadblocks, continued to restrict population movements, hinder access to basic services and livelihoods, and heighten protection risks for affected communities.

The situation remained volatile, with at least 11 improvised explosive devices (IED) incidents recorded during the reporting period, including 10 in the North-West and one in the South-West. While these attacks primarily targeted SSFs and their convoys, civilians remained at significant risk of injury or death from accidental explosions.

Attacks and threats against education intensified ahead of the 2026/2027 school year. NSAGs enforced school-related restrictions, imposed school levies in some areas, and increased intimidation of education personnel, including the abduction of five teachers in Wum (Menchum division, North-West). In September, armed actors also attacked a secondary school in the North-West, disrupting learning activities.

Humanitarian needs remained severe across the two regions, exacerbated by successive lockdowns imposed by NSAGs between 1 and 21 September. The measures restricted movement, disrupted education, livelihoods, and economic activities and limited access to essential services. Lockdown enforcement through threats and sporadic attacks resulted in civilian casualties in both regions and further affected already vulnerable communities.

Continued clashes between parties to the crisis triggered new population displacement and humanitarian needs across the North-West and South-West. In Momo division, an estimated 875 people (175 households) were displaced from Diku to Tikom during the reporting period with many families seeking refuge in nearby bushes. Heavy rainfall that caused flooding and landslides on 5 August affected over 4,157 people, displaced more than 500, caused five reported deaths, including a pregnant woman, and destroyed or damaged 16 houses infrastructure, livestock, and community water systems in Limbe (Fako division), Kumba (Meme division) in the South-West, and in Tinifoimbi Village (Boyo division) in the North-West. While many affected households have returned, those whose shelters were destroyed or damaged remain displaced and in need of assistance. Priority needs include shelter, food assistance, health, WASH, protection, education and livelihood support. In coordination with OCHA and area-based coordination co-chairs, humanitarian partners delivered multipurpose cash assistance, shelter support, psychosocial services, and gender-based violence prevention interventions across affected communities, in addition to the assistance delivered by authorities.

Humanitarian access remained constrained due to insecurity, prolonged lockdown and the presence of illegal checkpoints along key road corridors, including the Bamenda-Widikum axis in Momo division and the Bamenda-Ndop road. These restrictions significantly hindered population movements and limited the transportation of agricultural produce. The operational environment remained highly challenging and required continuous access negotiations amid a fragile, volatile, and rapidly evolving context.

items.author: Save the Children
items.content:
Country: World
Source: Save the Children

MANILA, 18 November 2026 - Governments announced more than 250 new commitments to prevent violence against children at a key global summit on child protection in Manila, with Save the Children urging leaders to turn those promises into funded action.

At the second Global Ministerial Conference to End Violence Against Children (EVAC), representatives from over 80 of the 130 countries present [1] made pledges across a range of areas, from combatting the recruitment and use of children in armed conflict and tech facilitated violence, to expanding child protection services to helping children recover from abuse.

Almost 40% of the countries making pledges did so for the first time, underscoring growing global momentum to make children safer, said Save the Children.

The new pledges come at a critical time for children, as conflict, climate shocks, poverty and inequality continue to expose millions of children to violence in their homes, schools, online and in their communities.

Violence against children encompasses any form of physical, emotional, digital or online abuse, sexual abuse, neglect, exploitation, or harmful traditional practices directed at children.

Every year, an estimated 1.6 billion children experience violence globally, including 90 million who experience sexual violence.[2], which can have lifelong consequences for children's health, learning, development, and wellbeing.

While progress has been made in recent years, far too many children still face violence every day, with devastating and often lifelong consequences for their health, wellbeing and future opportunities.

Save the Children urged leaders to turn promises into funded action.

Rebecca Smith, Global Head of Child Protection, Save the Children, said:

“We know how to prevent violence against children, now we need real commitment to make their safety a reality. These new pledges are a very welcome and important step forward, but they must now be backed by sustained investment, strong accountability and meaningful action that reaches children, wherever they live in the world, because millions of children continue to experience abuse, exploitation and harm every single day and their safety cannot be an afterthought. Children’s experiences and their voices must be at the heart of all violence prevention and survivor support initiatives.”

In 2025, Save the Children’s programmes reached 5.5 million children and caregivers globally through violence prevention and response interventions.

Financial stress on families can increase the risk of violence against children. Through our Money Matters Toolkit Save the Children helps caseworkers to engage families in conversations about budgeting and financial decision-making to help families make informed decisions and be more resilient.

Save the Children’s Safe Families initiative works with children of all ages, caregivers and communities to support families to better communicate and solve problems together, encourage adults to better understand child development and see children as rights holders with their own views and perspectives with separate sessions just for children.

items.content:
Country: Côte d'Ivoire
Source: World Food Programme

Please refer to the attached files.

*Enhancing the climate-adaptive capacity of smallholder farming communities
in the Poro Region, focusing on vulnerable women and youth*

Context

Climate shocks are undermining food systems in
northern regions of Côte d’Ivoire, such as Poro. Since
the 1980s, this region has experienced erratic rainfall
patterns, resulting in repeated drought episodes and a
gradual decline in average annual precipitation.
These challenges are becoming more severe as
temperatures continue to rise and weather patterns
become less predictable. Combined with recurrent
droughts and land degradation, they are significantly
reducing agricultural productivity in a region where
livelihoods depend heavily on rain-fed agriculture.
Women farmers, who play a central role in local food
systems, continue to face systemic barriers to
accessing land, water, financial services, and climate
information. These challenges limit their ability to adapt
to climate shocks, strengthen their productivity, and
build resilient livelihoods.
Climate projections indicate that the share of arable
land affected by drought could increase from 7% in
2000 to 23% by 2080, leading to yield declines of up
to 9% for maize and 10% for millet and sorghum.
This would further exacerbate food insecurity and
livelihood vulnerabilities.
Climate shocks are therefore not a future risk;
they are a current threat to food security,
livelihoods, and economic empowerment of
women and youth.

items.title: Mali: People returning from gold-panning sites in Guinea get help on arrival
items.author: International Committee of the Red Cross
items.content:
Countries: Mali, Guinea
Source: International Committee of the Red Cross

Bamako (CRM/ICRC) – At the beginning of November 2026, over 160,000 people crossed into Mali from Guinea at short notice, following the closure of the gold-panning areas of northern Guinea where they were working.

Exhausted after covering long distances on foot, they are staying at several locations in Mali. Many arrived with nothing to live on.

On 5 November, volunteers from the Mali Red Cross (Croix-Rouge malienne, CRM), responded to this sudden humanitarian emergency by deploying to the Bamako and Kourémalé reception sites and the Sikasso and Bougouni transit points, so they could begin meeting people’s most urgent needs.

“Our teams are active in a number of areas: food, water, first aid, psycho-social support, restoring family links, sanitation and hygiene,” says CRM Director-General Nouhoum Maiga. “We are working closely with the national and local authorities, especially the National Social Development Department, which is coordinating reception and assistance efforts.”

The ICRC and other partners within the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement are supporting the response, in particular the Red Cross Societies of Belgium, Denmark, Luxembourg and the Netherlands.

“The CRM is providing emergency aid to people affected by this crisis, with the support of the ICRC,” says Nicolas Lambert who heads the ICRC’s Mali delegation. “The ICRC has also supplied a number of government facilities with emergency medical kits. This temporary support will ensure that the most vulnerable people receive the care they need as exceptional numbers arrived over a short period.”

Operational update

Health

The ICRC has provided the CRM with the following medical supplies, enabling the National Society to respond to the returnees’ most urgent health needs:

  • Six large medical kits, including medicines (anti-malarial drugs, antibiotics, painkillers, anti-parasite medication, anti-fungal medication, etc.), dressings, gloves, compresses and disinfectant. These kits, designed to treat 6,000 sick or wounded patients for three months, have been allocated as follows: two to the Bamako Civil Defence Department, three to the Mali Red Cross and one to Bougouni Regional Health Department.
  • Two dressing kits, including antiseptic, bandages, compresses, cotton wool, gloves, serums and items for treating burns. These were handed over to the Bamako Civil Defence Department. Each kit is designed to treat 15 to 25 people with minor injuries.
  • Two kits for the care of people with serious injuries, including antibiotics, painkillers, dressing material, sterilization supplies, surgical and examination gloves, serums and disinfectant. These were delivered to Bougouni Regional Health Department. Each kit is designed to treat 25 people with serious injuries.
  • One kit for the care of people with serious injuries and 250 doses of saline solution for Kati University Hospital.

Food

The ICRC immediately provided the CRM with funds to help it serve daily hot meals to thousands of people in distress. Between 5 and 14 November, CRM volunteers distributed over 27,800 hot meals, over 30,000 packs of water and 18,000 loaves of milk bread in Bamako and the surrounding area.

Restoring family links

As of 14 November, 536 phone calls had been facilitated, enabling people to re-establish contact with their families.

Technical support

ICRC teams are providing advice and guidance to CRM personnel as they handle this emergency. Topics include the protection of vulnerable groups, health, sanitation and waste management.

Organisations impartiales, neutres et indépendantes, la CRM et le CICR agissent au Mali en partenariat étroit, main dans la main, afin de répondre au mieux aux besoins humanitaires les plus criants.

The Mali Red Cross

The CRM is a non-profit humanitarian organization. It was founded on 20 August 1965, on the basis of the Geneva Conventions of August 1949 and in accordance with Regulation 59 PCG of 28 March 1959 governing associations and NGOs in the Republic of Mali. The Malian government recognized the CRM as a public utility by Decree No. 123 of 13 September 1965. It is an auxiliary to the public authorities but operates independently of them.

The CRM has been helping vulnerable people for over 60 years, thanks to the unwavering commitment of its dynamic network of over 10,000 altruistic women and men all over the country and the steadfast support of its partners.

The ICRC in Mali

The ICRC has been carrying out humanitarian work in Mali since 1965 and has had a permanent presence in the country since 1991 under a headquarters agreement. Against the backdrop of persistent violence and armed conflict, especially in the centre and north of the country, and increased pressure on essential public services, the ICRC runs its activities in Mali from its delegation in Bamako, with subdelegations in Mopti, Timbuktu and Gao, offices in Kidal and Ménaka, and a satellite office in Niafounké. It works in the areas most affected by fighting, as close as possible to the people affected.

The ICRC works closely and entirely transparently with national, regional and local authorities. It also maintains a close partnership with the Mali Red Cross and other components of the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Movement.
